title: Intrinsic Credit Assignment for Long Horizon Interaction
claim: Rewarding intermediate belief changes gives a denser credit signal than outcome-only reward, yielding faster and better training.
layout: 2 stacked panels: method diagram on top, training curve below; banner links them
description: The top half contrasts two levels of credit assignment, separated by a dashed vertical line. On the left, pink boxes (Turn 1, Turn 2, ..., Turn N, Outcome) are chained by arrows. A black bracket arrow feeds back from Outcome to every turn, showing a single trajectory-level reward. On the right, a large rounded blue box labeled 'ΔBelief Reward' shows two small bar histograms, for turn t+1 and turn t. The target answer's bar is highlighted in blue, and a minus sign sits between the histograms. Log-probability formulas sit above them, and 'Change in agent's beliefs' sits below. Blue arrows of different shades point from this box to each turn. A banner reads 'Intrinsic Credit Assignment → Better Training Signal'. Below it, a line plot of success rate against training step shows ΔBelief-RL (blue) rising above GRPO (pink), which declines late in training.
caption: \looseness -1 Main contributions. We propose a dense reward signal, \RewardOur{} Reward, based on agent intrinsic belief updates in long horizon tasks. We find that (1) \MethodOur{} leads to more sample-efficient training (2) our trained agent generalizes better to unseen information-seeking tasks; and (3) scales better with increased test-time interaction budget.
abstract: How can we train agents to navigate uncertainty over long horizons? In this work, we propose ÎBelief-RL, which leverages a language model's own intrinsic beliefs to reward intermediate progress. Our method utilizes the change in the probability an agent assigns to the target solution for credit assignment. By training on synthetic interaction data, ÎBelief-RL teaches information-seeking capabilities that consistently outperform purely outcome-based rewards for Reinforcement Learning, with improvements generalizing to out-of-distribution applications ranging from customer service to personalization. Notably, the performance continues to improve as we scale test-time interactions beyond the training horizon, with interaction-efficiency increasing even on Pass@k metrics. Overall, our work introduces a scalable training strategy for navigating uncertainty over a long-horizon, by enabling credit assignment to intermediate actions via intrinsic ÎBelief rewards.
